This convergence arises because of the limited range of BEVs compared to the daily service profile for AV fleet operations as well as the corresponding increased time for recharging (i.e., refueling) the vehicle. Each vehicle’s batteries will need to be recharged at some point, which in turn takes the vehicle out of service anywhere from minutes to hours during the daily period of operations. In comparison, a fleet of vehicles propelled by internal combustion engines typically carries enough fuel on board for a full day’s duty cycle. If needed, the vehicles can refuel in a relatively short amount of time. Further, the trend of transit industry thinking is that for the very largest vehicles (40-passenger buses or larger), fuels such as hydrogen fuel cells or liquified natural gas are also being considered for AV technology applications. However, for the small- to medium- sized AV deployments carrying between 2 and 20 passengers per vehicle, BEV propulsion systems remain the most commonly preferred choice. As battery technology improves and corresponding rapid charging technology progresses, these issues may self-mitigate. However, for any near-term deployment, the practical limitations of EV range and corresponding battery charging considerations must be integrated into the overall service design of any AMD AV fleet service. A charging strategy that considers both EV battery characteristics and the associated charging infrastructure is critical for any AMD effort. This strategy includes accounting for the nonlinear nature of battery charging rates over the extent of the battery charge level. The charging rate varies throughout the charging process. The first 20% charge for a fully depleted EV battery 45 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. occurs at a significantly slower pace than the charging rate above 20%. Similarly, the charging rate above an 80% charge level is also significantly slower. For this reason, the time allowance for battery charging of a public fleet vehicle is often scheduled for charging only between 20% and 80% charge level. This nonlinear battery charging characteristic, combined with the high cost of charging infrastructure and any associated power distribution upgrade, requires a thorough analysis and design process. The charging strategy for EV fleets serving an AMD determines the design of the charging station size (number of vehicle positions), capacity (power requirements for the composite charging station power demands), and configuration (vehicle positions and access/egress provisions). This is even more critical for AV fleets operated in on-demand service modes because the charging needs of an ODT system are not as predictable from day to day as those of fixed-route systems. As such, the infrastructure size, location, and configuration to service ODT fleets may be substantially different from those of fixed-route service operations.
